Epidemiology & Classification.title: Glioma Grading and Molecular Classification
Epidemiology & Classification.html:
Brain tumors come in two broad flavors: tumors that start in the brain (primary tumors, like gliomas) and tumors that spread there from cancer elsewhere in the body (brain metastases). This section covers how each is classified and how common they are, the foundation you need before workup, imaging, and treatment make sense.

What Is a Glioma, and Why Don't They Have a "Stage"?

Gliomas are primary tumors of the central nervous system (CNS) that arise from glial cells: the supportive cells of the nervous system, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglial cells. They are the most common cause of primary CNS malignancy. Unlike most cancers you've learned about, gliomas typically do not spread outside the CNS, so the TNM staging system (which tracks nodal spread and distant metastasis) doesn't apply. Instead, gliomas are described by their WHO grade, a scale from I to IV that reflects how aggressive the tumor looks and behaves biologically, lower grades tend to grow slowly and behave less aggressively, while higher grades grow quickly and carry a worse prognosis. Grade is a statement about intrinsic tumor biology, not about how far the tumor has traveled.

The WHO 2021 Classification: Molecular Markers Now Define the Diagnosis

Glioma classification used to rely purely on how the tumor looked under the microscope (histology). The 2016 WHO update (4th edition) began incorporating molecular features, and the 2021 WHO classification (5th edition) completed this shift. Adult-type diffuse gliomas are now organized primarily around a single defining test: IDH (isocitrate dehydrogenase) mutation status.

  • Glioblastoma (GBM) is, by definition, IDH wild-type.
  • IDH-mutant tumors are subclassified as either oligodendrogliomas (if they also have 1p/19q codeletion) or astrocytomas (if 1p/19q is intact).
  • Critically, an IDH-mutant astrocytoma that looks histologically like a grade 4 tumor is no longer called "glioblastoma": it is named "astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4." This matters because IDH-mutant tumors, even at high grade, behave and are prognosed differently than true (IDH-wildtype) GBM.
MarkerWhat it tells youClassification role
IDH mutationIndependent positive prognostic factor associated with improved overall survivalGBM = IDH wild-type; astrocytoma/oligodendroglioma = IDH mutant
1p/19q codeletionWhole-arm loss of chromosome arms 1p and 19q (an unbalanced translocation)Defining feature of oligodendroglioma
ATRX lossMutually exclusive with 1p/19q codeletionCharacteristic of diffuse astrocytomas
TP53 mutationMissense mutation common in IDH-mutant tumorsAlso characteristic of diffuse astrocytomas
Clinical Pearl Memorize the WHO 2021 logic as a single decision tree: is the tumor IDH wild-type or mutant? If wild-type → GBM. If mutant, is 1p/19q codeleted? If yes → oligodendroglioma; if no (and ATRX/TP53 altered) → astrocytoma. This one branch point explains most glioma nomenclature you'll encounter.

Histologic Grading: The "MEAN" Features

Even though molecular markers now drive classification, histology still matters for grading. Pathologists look for four features, remembered by the mnemonic MEAN (or AMEN): nuclear Atypia, Mitotic index, Endothelial proliferation, and Necrosis. The more of these features present, the higher the grade. Glioblastoma is defined histologically by the presence of three of these features (with microvascular/endothelial proliferation) and/or the pathognomonic finding of "pseudopalisading" necrosis: tumor cells lining up densely around necrotic zones like a fence.

Molecular Findings That Bump the Grade to IV

The 2021 update also allows certain molecular findings to override histology and assign WHO grade IV even when the tumor doesn't look that aggressive under the microscope. An IDH-wildtype tumor that looks histologically grade 2 or 3 is assigned WHO grade IV if it has any one of: EGFR amplification, combined whole chromosome 7 gain and chromosome 10 loss, or a TERT promoter mutation. Separately, an IDH-mutant grade 2–3 tumor is upgraded to WHO grade IV (as "astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade IV") if it has a CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion. The takeaway: molecular biology can be a worse prognostic signal than what the tumor looks like on the slide.

Epidemiology: How Common Are These Tumors?

Glioblastoma is the most common primary CNS malignancy in adults, accounting for roughly 80% of primary CNS malignancies. It typically presents at a median age of ~65 years, with a slight male predominance (~3:2). Despite treatment, prognosis remains poor, with a median overall survival of only ~14 months. Among high-grade gliomas overall, grade III (anaplastic) tumors make up about 25%, with anaplastic astrocytoma being more common than anaplastic oligodendroglioma (which is comparatively more frequent in pediatric patients). Low-grade gliomas (grade I–II) are an uncommon, heterogeneous group that tends to affect younger adults and children.

Brain metastases are a completely different epidemiologic story: they are the most common intracranial tumor in adults overall, accounting for more than half of all brain tumors. Somewhere between 20–40% of all cancer patients will develop intracranial metastases during their disease course, and about 80% of those patients have multiple lesions at diagnosis. In adults, the most common primary cancers that metastasize to brain are lung, breast, kidney, colorectal, and melanoma; in children, think sarcomas, neuroblastoma, and germ cell tumors.

Clinical Pearl Don't confuse "most common primary CNS tumor" with "most common brain tumor overall." Glioblastoma is the most common primary CNS malignancy in adults, but brain metastases outnumber all primary CNS tumors combined, making up over 50% of intracranial tumors seen in adult practice.

Workup & Staging.title: Diagnostic Workup of CNS Tumors
Workup & Staging.html:
Before any treatment decision can be made, a suspected brain tumor has to be characterized: what does it look like, is it primary or metastatic, and, for gliomas especially, what does its molecular fingerprint look like? This section walks through how that workup unfolds in practice.

Clinical Presentation and Initial Evaluation

Patients with CNS tumors, whether primary or metastatic, typically present with neurological symptoms: headaches, focal neurologic deficits, seizures, or confusion. The initial evaluation is a full history and physical exam with a focus on the neurologic exam, including a fundoscopic exam if there is concern for increased intracranial pressure (papilledema is a key finding to look for). Baseline labs (CBC, CMP) help assess for other causes of symptoms and establish a baseline before any chemotherapy that could cause cytopenias.

Imaging Workup

Imaging proceeds in a deliberate sequence. A non-contrast CT head is obtained first and quickly, its main job is to rule out an acute intracranial bleed, which would change management immediately. Once bleeding is excluded, an MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast is the definitive study, including T1 post-contrast (T1c/FSPGR) and T2 FLAIR sequences at minimum. MRI is what actually characterizes the lesion, its enhancement pattern, associated edema, and relationship to surrounding structures (see the Imaging doc for a full breakdown of what each sequence shows). Additional workup is tailored to presentation: an EEG if the patient has had seizures, and neurocognitive testing to establish a baseline before radiation or chemotherapy, both of which can affect cognition over time.

Differential Diagnosis of a CNS Mass

Not every mass on brain MRI is a primary glioma. The differential is broad, and organizing it helps you think systematically:

  • Neoplastic: metastatic tumor; primary CNS neoplasms, which are further split into extra-axial lesions arising from outside the brain parenchyma (meningioma, schwannoma) and intra-axial lesions arising within the brain parenchyma itself (glial tumors, primary CNS lymphoma).
  • Non-neoplastic: infectious (e.g., abscess), inflammatory, toxic/metabolic, and genetic etiologies can all mimic a tumor on imaging.

This distinction between intra-axial and extra-axial location is a useful first mental checkpoint any time you're looking at a new brain mass.

Establishing a Tissue Diagnosis and Molecular Testing

For suspected primary gliomas, tissue is obtained via maximal safe resection or biopsy (discussed further in the Treatment doc). That tissue is then run through both standard histopathology (grading via the MEAN/AMEN criteria) and molecular testing: IDH mutation status, 1p/19q codeletion, ATRX, TP53, and MGMT promoter methylation status: because these results directly determine both the diagnosis and the treatment plan. MGMT (O-6 methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase) deserves special attention: it's a DNA repair enzyme that removes the methyl groups that alkylating chemotherapy (like temozolomide) deposits on guanine bases. High MGMT expression means the tumor can repair this damage efficiently and resists chemotherapy. When the MGMT promoter is methylated, however, the gene is silenced, MGMT protein isn't made, the tumor can't repair TMZ-induced damage, and the tumor responds better to treatment, making MGMT methylation a strong positive prognostic factor and a predictor of chemotherapy benefit.

Timing matters for postoperative imaging too: a postoperative MRI brain with and without gadolinium should be obtained 24–48 hours after surgery (72 hours maximum) to accurately assess extent of resection. Wait longer than that, and maturing blood products in and around the surgical cavity start to enhance on their own, confounding the picture and making it hard to tell residual tumor from postsurgical change.

Clinical Pearl MGMT promoter methylation is one of the highest-yield concepts in neuro-oncology: it predicts response to temozolomide across LGG, anaplastic glioma, and GBM, and is even used to guide treatment decisions in elderly/frail GBM patients (methylated tumors may be treated with TMZ alone).

Workup for Brain Metastases

Unlike a primary glioma, a brain metastasis always requires a tissue diagnosis of cancer: imaging alone is not sufficient for definitive management decisions. In practice this plays out two ways: if a patient has a known history of metastatic cancer (e.g., lung cancer) and develops a new brain lesion with a classic appearance, imaging plus clinical context may be enough to proceed. But if there is no known history of malignancy, the workup expands to a CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis to find the primary, along with biopsy of the most accessible site, which may be the brain lesion itself via maximal safe resection, or another, easier-to-reach metastatic site.

MRI with and without contrast is the gold standard imaging study. On T1 pre-contrast, metastases are typically iso- to hypointense (though hemorrhagic mets can show intrinsic high signal). On T1 post-contrast, they enhance in a uniform, punctate, or ring pattern and are usually hyperintense. T2/FLAIR highlights the surrounding vasogenic edema, which is often disproportionately large relative to the tumor itself.

Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis is a distinct and more ominous entity, where cancer cells invade the cerebrospinal fluid and coat the meninges. It presents with a broad symptom mix, pain, seizures, nausea/vomiting, ataxia, cranial nerve deficits, incontinence, and is diagnosed by MRI (nodular meningeal tumor, meningeal thickening, strong enhancement) combined with CSF analysis (positive cytology, elevated opening pressure, elevated protein, and pleocytosis).

Prognostic Tools for Brain Metastases

Because treatment choice for brain mets (surgery vs. SRS vs. WBRT) depends heavily on expected survival, prognostic scoring systems play a central clinical role, more so than in most other cancers. The RTOG Recursive Partitioning Analysis (RPA, 1997) stratifies patients using KPS, age, and extent of extracranial disease. The Graded Prognostic Assessment (GPA, 2008) built on this by adding the number of CNS metastases as an independent prognostic factor. Most recently, the Diagnosis-Specific GPA (2020), derived from a multi-institutional database of nearly 7,000 patients, provides a disease-specific tool (available at brainmetgpa.com) to individualize survival estimates and treatment planning.

Imaging.title: MRI Patterns in Brain Tumors
Imaging.html:
MRI is how radiation oncologists "see" a brain tumor, it doesn't just detect a mass, it tells you what kind of mass it probably is, how aggressive it likely is, and, after treatment, whether it's really growing back. This section builds the visual vocabulary you'll use constantly on rounds and in clinic.

MRI Sequences: What Each One Actually Shows

A brain MRI protocol for tumor imaging is really a stack of different physics experiments layered on the same anatomy, and each sequence answers a different question.

  • T1 (pre-contrast) shows basic anatomy; tumor tissue is usually hypo- to isointense and mostly useful as a baseline for comparison.
  • T1 post-contrast (T1+C) is the single most important sequence for grading and for radiation target delineation. Enhancement occurs where gadolinium contrast leaks through a disrupted blood-brain barrier (BBB): so enhancement is a marker of BBB breakdown, which tends to track with higher-grade, more aggressive tumor biology.
  • T2/FLAIR highlights edema and infiltrative tumor signal, this is what shows you how far a tumor's influence extends beyond the enhancing core, and it's essential for defining radiation treatment volumes in gliomas.
  • DWI/ADC (diffusion-weighted imaging) measures how freely water molecules move. Restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, dark on ADC) indicates densely packed cells, think high cellularity/tumor, while facilitated diffusion is more typical of necrosis or treatment effect, where cells have broken down and water moves more freely.
  • Perfusion imaging (rCBV, relative cerebral blood volume) is a proxy for how much new blood vessel growth (neovascularity) is happening in a region. Elevated rCBV suggests high-grade tumor or true tumor progression; low rCBV favors treatment effect.

Put together, these sequences let you triangulate: does this look like tumor (enhances, restricts diffusion, high rCBV) or treatment effect (facilitated diffusion, low rCBV)?

Glioblastoma: The Ring-Enhancing, Necrotic Mass

Glioblastoma has a classic and highly recognizable MRI appearance: thick, irregular ring enhancement surrounding a central necrotic core. This pattern mirrors the histologic hallmark of GBM, "pseudopalisading" necrosis is fairly unique to this tumor, and the imaging ring corresponds to viable, hypervascular tumor rim surrounding a dying center that has outgrown its blood supply. The surrounding vasogenic edema on T2/FLAIR is not just reactive swelling, it is itself infiltrated by tumor cells, which is part of why GBM is so difficult to fully resect or contain within a radiation field. GBM can also cross the corpus callosum to involve both hemispheres, producing the classic "butterfly glioma" appearance. On perfusion imaging, rCBV is elevated, and susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) often shows microhemorrhage (intratumoral susceptibility signal, ITSS).

A few mimics are worth knowing how to separate from GBM: a brain abscess has a smooth, complete rim on SWI with central restricted diffusion (the opposite of GBM's irregular, incomplete rim with facilitated diffusion centrally); an IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytoma (which is not called GBM, per the WHO 2021 classification) often shows the distinctive T2/FLAIR mismatch sign; and CNS lymphoma typically enhances homogeneously, without the necrosis that defines GBM.

Low-Grade vs. High-Grade Gliomas

The single most useful discriminator between low-grade and high-grade gliomas on imaging is contrast enhancement. Low-grade gliomas (LGG) classically do not enhance: "no enhancement is the rule." They appear as T2/FLAIR hyperintense regions with minimal or no surrounding edema, normal perfusion, and normal MR spectroscopy, consistent with their indolent biology. If a previously non-enhancing LGG develops new enhancement, that is a major red flag for malignant transformation to a higher-grade tumor and should prompt reassessment. High-grade gliomas, in contrast, enhance, show elevated rCBV, tend to have more surrounding edema, and, in the case of GBM specifically, demonstrate necrosis.

Brain Metastases vs. Primary Glial Tumors

Distinguishing a solitary brain metastasis from a primary glioma matters enormously for workup and management, and imaging offers real clues even before biopsy. Metastases are classically multiple and centered at the gray-white matter junction: a direct consequence of how they get there: tumor cells embolize hematogenously and lodge where blood vessels narrow at this junction. Metastases show heterogeneous enhancement with small necrotic foci, and, distinctively, their surrounding edema is disproportionately large relative to the size of the lesion itself, unlike the more edema-proportionate pattern typical of gliomas. Perfusion imaging can help too: rCBV in the edema surrounding a metastasis tends to be lower than the rCBV in the edema surrounding a GBM (glioma edema is infiltrated by tumor; metastasis edema generally is not). One useful special case: melanoma metastases are T1-hyperintense due to the paramagnetic properties of melanin, which can help suggest the primary before pathology confirms it.

Pseudoprogression vs. True Progression

This distinction is one of the trickiest and highest-yield concepts in neuro-oncologic imaging. After chemoradiation for GBM, a follow-up MRI can show new or enlarging enhancement that looks alarming, but in a substantial fraction of patients (pseudoprogression rates have been reported around 30–40%), this represents pseudoprogression: transiently increased vascular permeability and inflammation triggered by radiation (and possibly worsened by concurrent temozolomide), not true tumor regrowth. Pseudoprogression occurs mainly within the first ~3 months after completing chemoradiation, and it typically improves on follow-up imaging without any change in treatment. The imaging signature helps distinguish it from real progression: pseudoprogression shows facilitated diffusion, low rCBV, and MR spectroscopy with elevated lactate but without elevated choline; true progression shows elevated rCBV and rising choline (choline is a marker of cell membrane turnover/proliferation). Interestingly, MGMT promoter-methylated tumors are more prone to pseudoprogression: plausibly because they are also more chemo/radiosensitive to begin with.

Clinical Pearl New enhancement in a previously non-enhancing low-grade glioma is a red flag for malignant transformation, never dismiss it as an imaging artifact.
Clinical Pearl When you see growing enhancement within the first 3 months after chemoRT for GBM, think pseudoprogression before true progression, especially if the tumor is MGMT-methylated, check rCBV (low favors pseudoprogression) and consider a short-interval follow-up MRI rather than immediately declaring treatment failure.

Treatment Paradigms: Gliomas.title: Treatment Paradigms for Gliomas
Treatment Paradigms: Gliomas.html:
Glioma treatment is built around the same three tools: surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. How they're combined, in what dose, and for how long changes dramatically depending on the tumor's grade and molecular profile. This section walks through management by grade, from low-grade gliomas through the full glioblastoma protocol.

Low-Grade Glioma (WHO Grade I–II) Management

Management of low-grade glioma starts, as with all gliomas, with maximal safe resection: removing as much tumor as possible while preserving neurologic function, since extent of resection correlates with prognosis.

  • Gross total resection + low-risk features → observation with close follow-up (avoids radiation toxicity in patients who may do well for years)
  • High-risk by Pignatti "SATAN" criteria (Size ≥6cm, Age >40, Tumor crossing midline, Astrocytoma histology, Neurologic symptoms) → adjuvant radiation, 54 Gy/30 fractions
  • High-risk, after radiation → add chemotherapy: PCV (procarbazine/CCNU/vincristine) x6 cycles, or temozolomide, both improve progression-free and overall survival

Risk of recurrence is real even in "low-risk" patients: in one study, patients under 40 with LGG had a >50% risk of recurrence at 5 years.

Anaplastic (Grade III) Glioma Management

Grade III gliomas split into two treatment pathways depending on molecular subtype.

  • Anaplastic oligodendroglioma (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q codeleted) → radiation 59.4 Gy/33 fx + adjuvant PCV (the OS benefit from adding PCV is greatest specifically in this codeleted population)
  • Anaplastic astrocytoma (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q intact, ATRX/TP53 altered) → radiation 59.4 Gy/33 fx + adjuvant temozolomide (survival benefit is specific to IDH-mutant tumors, not IDH-wildtype)
  • Either subtype → concurrent TMZ (given during radiation, as in the GBM protocol) adds no benefit here; only the adjuvant course matters

Anaplastic gliomas are molecularly heterogeneous: what helps a 1p/19q codeleted tumor doesn't necessarily help a 1p/19q intact one, and giving concurrent chemotherapy when it offers no benefit only adds toxicity.

Glioblastoma: The Stupp Protocol, Step by Step

GBM management follows a well-defined, sequential protocol, often just called "the Stupp protocol" after the trial that established it (see the Literature doc).

  • Step 1, surgery → maximal safe resection while preserving neurologic function; subtotal resection/debulking or stereotactic biopsy if GTR isn't safely achievable (deep-seated, eloquent-area, or multifocal tumors)
  • Step 2, concurrent chemoradiation → 60 Gy in 30 fractions to the postoperative cavity/residual tumor plus surrounding T2 FLAIR edema, daily Monday–Friday for ~6 weeks, with temozolomide 75 mg/m²/day, all 7 days a week, throughout; add PCP prophylaxis (pentamidine or TMP-SMX) and monitor for cytopenias
  • Step 3 → ~4-week treatment break to recover before the more intensive adjuvant phase
  • Step 4, adjuvant (maintenance) therapy → temozolomide 150–200 mg/m²/day for 5 days, every 28 days for 6 cycles, plus Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields), worn 18+ hours/day until second radiographic progression or up to 2 years (supratentorial tumors only)

Adjusting for Elderly and Frail Patients

  • Age roughly 60–70, otherwise healthy → standard 60 Gy/30 fx + TMZ remains standard of care
  • Poorer performance status → hypofractionated RT (40 Gy/15 fx, 34 Gy/10 fx, or 25 Gy/5 fx) ± TMZ
  • Poor performance status + MGMT promoter-methylated tumor → TMZ alone (no radiation) is a reasonable option
Clinical Pearl The GBM treatment sequence is a four-part pattern worth memorizing cold: surgery → concurrent chemoRT (60 Gy/30 fx + daily low-dose TMZ) → treatment break → adjuvant TMZ (higher dose, monthly cycles) + TTFields. Know why each phase exists, not just the numbers.
Clinical Pearl For anaplastic gliomas: PCV benefits 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas most; adjuvant (not concurrent) TMZ benefits IDH-mutant astrocytomas. Concurrent TMZ has no proven benefit outside the GBM setting.

Treatment Paradigms: Brain Mets.title: Treatment Paradigms for Brain Metastases
Treatment Paradigms: Brain Mets.html:
Brain metastases are treated with a different mindset than primary gliomas: the CNS disease is usually only one part of the patient's overall cancer, so treatment choice constantly balances tumor control in the brain against preserving quality of life and cognition. This section covers the three main tools, surgery, SRS, and WBRT, and how oncologists choose among them.

Initial Supportive Care and the Three Treatment Modalities

  • Peritumoral edema / neurologic symptoms → corticosteroids (dexamethasone): IV loading dose, then scheduled dosing with a taper once definitive treatment begins (improves symptoms in ~75% of patients within 3 days); add PPI prophylaxis and glucose monitoring
  • Seizures → add anti-seizure medication
  • Large tumor causing significant edema/mass effect, or diagnosis uncertain → surgery
  • Small tumor(s), or multiple tumors not amenable to surgery (e.g., eloquent brain) → stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), pre-/postoperatively or standalone
  • Many metastases (e.g., >10), high disease volume, or leptomeningeal disease → whole brain radiotherapy (WBRT)

Whole Brain Radiotherapy: Dosing and Technique

  • Most common regimen → 30 Gy/10 fractions
  • Better prognosis (minimize late toxicity) → 35 Gy/14 fractions
  • Worse prognosis (palliative) → 20 Gy/5 fractions, just as effective palliatively with less time in treatment
  • Prophylactic cranial irradiation, small cell lung cancer → separate 25 Gy/10 fraction regimen
  • Long expected survival (toxicity will matter) → favor surgery/SRS over WBRT, or add hippocampal avoidance ± memantine if WBRT is necessary

Delivered via two parallel opposed lateral fields (the "German helmet field" technique) with thermoplastic mask immobilization; MLCs help spare the scalp and shield the lenses/facial structures. Main limitation: neurocognitive toxicity, especially short-term/delayed recall memory loss, becomes clinically evident at 4–6 months.

Stereotactic Radiosurgery: Indications and Dosing

  • Tumor ≤2 cm, single fraction → 24 Gy
  • Tumor 2–3 cm, single fraction → 18 Gy
  • Tumor 3–4 cm, single fraction → 15 Gy
  • Tumor >2 cm → fractionated SRS, 27 Gy in 3 fractions (better local control, less radiation necrosis than one large fraction)
  • Good SRS candidate → life expectancy >4–6 months, generally <15–20 metastases, and a cumulative volume small enough to meet whole-brain dose constraints
  • Post-surgical resection cavity → pre- or postoperative SRS improves local control vs. observation alone

Choosing Between SRS and WBRT

  • Good performance status, limited number of brain metastases → SRS alone is generally preferred; requires close MRI surveillance to catch new lesions early
  • Prioritizing maximal brain tumor control over cognition → WBRT (or WBRT added to SRS)

Across trials the tradeoff repeats: WBRT wins on brain tumor control, SRS wins on preserved cognition, and neither reliably wins on overall survival, since systemic disease, not the CNS disease, usually limits survival. Total volume of brain disease predicts survival better than the raw number of metastases.

Hippocampal Avoidance and Memantine

  • WBRT needed, metastases >5mm from the hippocampus → hippocampal avoidance (HA-WBRT): IMRT-based planning with a 5mm avoidance margin around the hippocampal subgranular zone (site of adult neurogenesis)
  • Any patient receiving WBRT → consider memantine (NMDA-receptor antagonist), titrated to 10mg twice daily over ~4 weeks, continued for 24 weeks total; reduces cognitive decline, particularly delayed recall
Clinical Pearl The size/number cutoffs worth memorizing: single-fraction SRS generally works best for lesions <2 cm (24 Gy); for >2 cm, fractionate (27 Gy/3 fx) to improve local control and reduce radiation necrosis. SRS candidacy is typically capped around 15–20 lesions, but total tumor volume matters more than raw number.
Clinical Pearl Across nearly every SRS-vs-WBRT comparison, the pattern repeats: WBRT wins on brain tumor control, SRS wins on preserved cognition, and neither reliably wins on overall survival. This tradeoff, not a "better" or "worse" therapy, is why treatment must be individualized to prognosis and patient priorities.

High-Yield Literature.title: Practice-Changing Trials in Neuro-Oncology
High-Yield Literature.html:
Neuro-oncology's treatment paradigms didn't come from nowhere, a handful of trials, repeated across decades, built the standards of care described elsewhere in these docs. Rather than re-deriving the full methodology of each one, this section focuses on the takeaway that matters: what did the trial show, and why did it change practice?

Low-Grade Glioma Trials

EORTC 22844 ("Believers' Trial") randomized patients to lower- vs. higher-dose radiation and found no benefit to dose escalation: 5-year OS and PFS were statistically identical between arms. Its lasting contribution was a multivariate analysis (the Pignatti "SATAN" criteria) identifying which patients are at higher risk of recurrence and thus most likely to benefit from adjuvant treatment. RTOG 9110 reached the same conclusion with an independent cohort: no OS or PFS benefit to high-dose vs. low-dose RT, even on 15-year follow-up.

EORTC 22845 ("Non-Believers' Trial") asked a different question, immediate RT after surgery vs. observation with RT deferred until progression. Immediate RT improved PFS and 1-year seizure control, but did not improve overall survival, likely because 75% of the observation arm eventually received RT anyway (salvage radiation worked). This established that upfront RT trades earlier toxicity for better disease control without necessarily buying more life.

RTOG 9802 had two parts. Its phase II observation component showed that even young, GTR patients face a >50% recurrence risk at 5 years, reinforcing that "low-risk" LGG still needs close follow-up. Its phase III component then showed that adding 6 cycles of adjuvant PCV after RT dramatically improved outcomes in high-risk LGG patients (10-year OS 60% vs. 40% without chemo), this trial is why chemotherapy became a standard addition to RT for high-risk LGG. RTOG 0424, a single-arm phase II study, showed favorable outcomes using concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide instead of PCV in high-risk LGG, though no trial has directly compared TMZ head-to-head against PCV in this setting.

Anaplastic (Grade III) Glioma Trials

The combined long-term analysis of RTOG 9402 and EORTC 26951 established that adding PCV to radiation improves OS and PFS in anaplastic oligodendroglioma, with the largest benefit concentrated in 1p/19q-codeleted tumors (20-year OS around 35% with RT + PCV in the codeleted subgroup), this is the trial basis for PCV as standard adjuvant chemotherapy in codeleted anaplastic oligodendroglioma. The original CODEL trial design (later redesigned) showed that TMZ alone was inferior to RT-containing arms, confirming radiation cannot be omitted for this histology.

NOA-04 tested whether the sequence of RT and chemotherapy mattered (RT first vs. chemo first) and found no difference in outcomes between sequencing strategies, but its more important finding was that IDH1 mutation status was a more powerful prognostic factor than 1p/19q codeletion or MGMT methylation, reinforcing the centrality of IDH status in glioma biology. CATNON then answered a key question for 1p/19q non-codeleted (astrocytoma-lineage) anaplastic gliomas: adjuvant TMZ improved OS substantially, but this benefit was seen only in IDH-mutant tumors, and concurrent TMZ added no benefit at all, whether alone or combined with adjuvant TMZ. This established the current standard of RT + adjuvant (not concurrent) TMZ for IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-intact anaplastic astrocytoma.

Glioblastoma Trials

The BTSG dose escalation study from the 1970s established 60 Gy/30 fx as the standard GBM radiation dose, patients receiving ≤45 Gy had worse outcomes. The single most important glioblastoma trial is the Stupp trial (EORTC, NEJM 2005): adding concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide to standard 60 Gy radiation improved median OS from 12.1 to 14.6 months and improved PFS, and this benefit held regardless of MGMT methylation status (though the effect was larger in methylated tumors), which is why TMZ became standard of care for essentially all newly diagnosed GBM patients, not just MGMT-methylated ones. The Stupp TTFields trial (JAMA 2017) then showed that adding Tumor Treating Fields to maintenance TMZ further improved both PFS (6.7 vs. 4.0 months) and OS (20.9 vs. 16 months), establishing TTFields as part of the modern standard maintenance regimen.

Not every trial changed practice. CeTeG/NOA-09 showed an OS benefit (but not a PFS benefit) to adding lomustine (CCNU) to standard RT-TMZ in MGMT-methylated GBM, but this combination has not been widely adopted due to concerns about added toxicity from dual chemotherapy and an underpowered analysis. Dose escalation and SRS/brachytherapy boost strategies have also been tested repeatedly (e.g., NRG-BN001, RTOG 9305) and have not shown benefit, outside of clinical trials, dose intensification is not currently used for GBM.

A cluster of trials (the Canadian trial, the Nordic trial, IAEA) established that elderly and frail patients may actually do worse with standard fractionation, and that hypofractionated regimens (e.g., 40 Gy/15 fx, 25 Gy/5 fx) achieve non-inferior outcomes with less treatment burden. Perry et al. (NEJM 2017) then showed that adding TMZ to hypofractionated RT (40 Gy/15 fx) in elderly patients still improved OS and PFS, with the largest benefit in MGMT-methylated tumors, this is the trial basis for combining hypofractionation with TMZ in appropriately selected elderly/frail patients rather than choosing one or the other.

Brain Metastasis Trials: Surgery and WBRT

The two Patchell trials shaped the modern approach to solitary brain metastasis. Patchell I showed that adding surgical resection before WBRT (compared to biopsy alone before WBRT) significantly improved local control, overall survival, and maintenance of performance status, establishing surgery's role for a resectable solitary metastasis. Patchell II then asked whether postoperative WBRT adds anything after resection: it significantly reduced both local and distant brain recurrence and reduced neurologic death, but did not improve overall survival, an important and recurring theme in brain-met literature, where better brain tumor control frequently does not translate into a longer life, because systemic disease usually determines survival first.

The QUARTZ trial tested a more provocative question in a poor-prognosis population: in NSCLC patients with brain metastases not suitable for surgery or SRS, does adding WBRT to best supportive care improve outcomes compared to supportive care alone? The answer was no, no significant difference in overall survival or quality-adjusted life-years, supporting a serious discussion of hospice/best supportive care in patients with very limited life expectancy rather than reflexively offering WBRT.

Brain Metastasis Trials: SRS and Cognition

A string of trials repeatedly explored the same tension: does adding WBRT to SRS (or choosing WBRT over SRS) buy better tumor control at the cost of cognition? RTOG 9508 showed that WBRT + SRS improved local control compared to WBRT alone in patients with limited metastases. JRSOG-99 compared SRS alone to SRS + WBRT and found SRS alone had worse local control and a higher rate of new brain metastases, but no difference in overall survival or neurologic death, SRS alone was suggested as a reasonable option for select patients with limited disease. The MDACC neurocognition trial (Chang et al.) sharpened the picture further: it closed early because the SRS + WBRT group showed significantly worse neurocognitive decline at 4 months than SRS alone, despite better local and distant brain control with WBRT added.

Alliance N0574 (RTOG 0671) is the pivotal modern trial: in patients with 1–3 brain metastases, SRS alone caused significantly less cognitive deterioration than SRS + WBRT (64% vs. 92%), with better quality of life, despite worse intracranial tumor control, and no difference in overall survival. This trial is why SRS alone is now the preferred strategy for good-performance-status patients with limited brain metastases, provided they can be followed closely for distant brain failure.

Beyond the classic "1–3 mets" teaching, JLGK0901 showed that SRS alone for 5–10 brain metastases was non-inferior in overall survival compared to 2–4 metastases, suggesting that total tumor volume, not raw number of lesions, is what really predicts outcomes, and that appropriately selected patients with more than a handful of small metastases can still be reasonable SRS candidates. For the postoperative setting, NCCTG N107C compared postoperative SRS to WBRT after resection and found better cognitive outcomes with SRS but worse local (surgical bed) control, again with no difference in overall survival, reinforcing that this is a genuine tradeoff, not a clearly "better" option.

Finally, NRG CC001 demonstrated that when WBRT truly is necessary, hippocampal-avoidance WBRT plus memantine significantly reduces the risk of cognitive decline compared to standard WBRT plus memantine alone, giving oncologists a concrete way to mitigate WBRT's biggest downside when it can't be avoided.

Clinical Pearl A theme runs through nearly all of the brain-metastasis literature: more aggressive brain-directed therapy (surgery, SRS + WBRT, WBRT itself) usually improves local or distant intracranial control, but rarely improves overall survival, because systemic disease, not the brain, usually determines how long a patient lives. This is exactly why toxicity and quality of life (especially cognition) have become the deciding factors in modern treatment selection.
Clinical Pearl If a trial name comes up on rounds and you only remember one fact, remember this: Stupp (2005) = TMZ + RT is standard for GBM regardless of MGMT status; Alliance N0574 = SRS alone preferred over SRS+WBRT for 1–3 mets due to cognition; Patchell II = postop WBRT improves local control, not survival.
